# Evolutionary SaaS Architecture: What the System Should Generate

**Analysis Subject**: Architecture of the SaaS applications GENERATED by the CLI tool
**Perspective**: Evolutionary architecture specialist — start simple, evolve on real signals
**Context**: Round 3, Branch 2.1 — Generated SaaS architecture knowledge
**Date**: 2026-03-12
**Scope**: NOT the CLI tool itself. The full-stack SaaS that the user receives and deploys.

---

## 0. Framing: Two Architectures, One System

There is a critical distinction that must not collapse:

- **The Generator** (CLI tool): Modular monolith, local-first, ~25 files (covered in Round 2)
- **The Generated SaaS** (what the user gets): A deployable, full-stack web application

Round 2 settled the generator's own architecture as evolutionary modular monolith. This analysis asks: **What architecture should the generator produce?** What SaaS architecture knowledge must be baked into the templates, scaffolding comments, and evolution guides?

The answer matters enormously. A generator that produces over-engineered SaaS will overwhelm users. A generator that produces naively simple SaaS will trap users when they grow. The evolutionary architecture approach threads this needle: generate the simplest thing that is also future-safe.

---

## 1. Initial MVP SaaS Architecture (Day 1 Generation)

### 1.1 Design Philosophy for the Generated Output

The generator must answer: **What is the minimum architecture a user needs to go from generated code to paying customer #1?**

That means:
- Auth that works in 30 minutes (Supabase Auth)
- A database that holds their data (Supabase PostgreSQL)
- A way to charge money (Stripe Checkout)
- A UI framework that is fast to modify (Next.js App Router + shadcn/ui)
- Deployment in under 10 minutes (Vercel one-click)

Nothing else on Day 1. No caching layer. No separate API service. No message queue. No CDN rules. Those are decisions deferred until the signals that require them actually appear.

### 1.2 Folder Structure: Exactly What Gets Generated

```

│   ├── (auth)/                   ← Route group: pre-auth pages

├── components/

```

**Total file count for a typical generated SaaS MVP**: 35–55 files depending on feature count. A 3-feature SaaS (e.g., project management, team invites, analytics dashboard) lands at approximately 48 files. This is intentionally below the cognitive overhead threshold where a solo developer starts losing mental model coherence.

### 1.3 What Is Deliberately Absent

The generator must NOT include, and must include comments explaining why they are absent:

| Absent Pattern | Why Absent | When to Add |
|----------------|------------|-------------|
| Redis / caching layer | Zero paying users cannot justify ops cost | >500 RPM on any route |
| Separate API service | No consumers yet | First enterprise API customer |
| Message queue (BullMQ, etc.) | No async tasks requiring durability | Batch jobs >30 seconds |
| Separate auth service | Supabase handles it completely | SAML/SSO enterprise requirement |
| Monorepo (Turborepo) | One product, one team, one deployment | Second product or second deployed service |
| Feature flags service | 2-3 plans can be hardcoded | >5 tiers, A/B testing requirement |
| Observability stack (Datadog, etc.) | Vercel Analytics + Supabase logs sufficient | Production incidents that need RCA |
| Database connection pooling | Supabase handles with PgBouncer | >50 concurrent connections sustained |

This absence list belongs in a generated `EVOLUTION.md` file (discussed in Section 5) so users understand the architecture decisions they inherited.

## 2. Data Layer: Schema Patterns That Allow Non-Breaking Evolution

### 2.1 The Four Universal Tables

Every generated SaaS starts with four tables. The generator writes these as the migration `0001_initial.sql`:

```sql
-- EVOLUTION NOTE: These four tables are the immutable core.
-- Never drop columns from them — add nullable columns only.
-- Extract to a separate 'organizations' service ONLY when you have
-- multi-product or M&A requirements. Signal: teams > 500 orgs.

CREATE TABLE users (
  id          UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email       TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  full_name   TEXT,
  avatar_url  TEXT,
  role        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'member' CHECK (role IN ('admin', 'member')),
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE organizations (
  id          UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  name        TEXT NOT NULL,
  slug        TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  -- EVOLUTION: Add plan_id FK to plans table when >3 pricing tiers needed
  plan        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'free' CHECK (plan IN ('free', 'pro', 'enterprise')),
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE organization_members (
  user_id     UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  org_id      UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES organizations(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  role        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'member' CHECK (role IN ('owner', 'admin', 'member')),
  joined_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, org_id)
);

CREATE TABLE subscriptions (
  id                TEXT PRIMARY KEY,  -- Stripe subscription ID
  org_id            UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES organizations(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  status            TEXT NOT NULL,     -- active, past_due, canceled, trialing
  price_id          TEXT NOT NULL,     -- Stripe price ID
  current_period_end TIMESTAMPTZ,
  cancel_at_period_end BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
  created_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
```

### 2.2 Domain Table Pattern

For each generated feature, the generator appends a domain migration:

```sql
-- EVOLUTION NOTE: This table follows the "soft-delete + audit" pattern.
-- Add soft_deleted_at before hard-deleting to enable recovery.
-- Add creator_id when you need attribution beyond org-level.
-- Extract to a separate service when this table exceeds 10M rows
-- AND query latency exceeds 200ms — not before.

CREATE TABLE [domain_entities] (
  id          UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  org_id      UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES organizations(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  -- domain-specific columns here
  created_by  UUID REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Row Level Security: org-scoped by default
ALTER TABLE [domain_entities] ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

CREATE POLICY "org_members_can_read"
  ON [domain_entities] FOR SELECT
  USING (
    org_id IN (
      SELECT org_id FROM organization_members
      WHERE user_id = auth.uid()
    )
  );
```

### 2.3 Supabase Tables vs Postgres Functions

The generator applies a simple rule, embedded as a comment in `lib/supabase/`:

```typescript
// ARCHITECTURE DECISION: When to use Supabase client vs Postgres functions
//
// Use Supabase client (tables + RLS):
//   - CRUD on single entity
//   - Simple joins (1-2 tables)
//   - Real-time subscriptions
//
// Use Postgres functions (via supabase.rpc()):
//   - Multi-step transactions (debit + credit, create + audit)
//   - Complex aggregations running in DB is faster than JS
//   - Operations that must be atomic
//
// NEVER use Postgres functions for:
//   - Simple reads that RLS covers
//   - Business logic that should be in Server Actions
//   (Postgres functions are hard to test and type-check)
```

### 2.4 File-Based Config vs Database Config

Pricing tiers and feature flags live in `lib/stripe/plans.ts` as TypeScript constants — not in the database. The generator hardcodes 2–3 tiers:

```typescript
// EVOLUTION NOTE: Plans are hardcoded until you have >5 tiers or A/B test
// pricing. Moving to DB-backed plans costs ~1 sprint and is only worth it
// when non-developers need to edit pricing without a deployment.
export const PLANS = {
  free:       { priceId: process.env.STRIPE_FREE_PRICE_ID,  features: [...] },
  pro:        { priceId: process.env.STRIPE_PRO_PRICE_ID,   features: [...] },
  enterprise: { priceId: process.env.STRIPE_ENT_PRICE_ID,   features: [...] },
} as const;

export type Plan = keyof typeof PLANS;
```

The benefit: zero database round-trips for plan lookups. The cost: a deployment is required to change pricing. For 0–1000 customers, this is the correct tradeoff.

## 3. Auth Layer: Simple Without Being Simplistic

### 3.1 Supabase Auth as the Starting Point

The generator configures Supabase Auth with email/password and two social providers (Google, GitHub by default, configurable). The middleware pattern ensures sessions are always fresh:

```typescript
// middleware.ts — generated at project root
// EVOLUTION NOTE: This is Supabase's recommended pattern.
// Replace with a separate auth service (Auth0, Clerk) ONLY when you need:
//   - SAML 2.0 / enterprise SSO
//   - Cross-product SSO (multiple apps, one login)
//   - Compliance requirements (SOC2 Type II, HIPAA)
// Before that point, Supabase Auth handles 99% of auth needs for <$100k ARR.
import { createServerClient } from '@supabase/ssr';
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server';
import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server';

export async function middleware(request: NextRequest) {
  // ... session refresh logic
}

export const config = {
  matcher: ['/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico).*)'],
};
```

### 3.2 RBAC: Simple Without Over-Engineering

Three roles: `owner`, `admin`, `member`. Encoded directly in `organization_members.role`. The generator produces guards in `lib/auth/guards.ts`:

```typescript
// EVOLUTION NOTE: This two-tier RBAC (org-level roles) handles 90% of SaaS
// needs up to ~500 customers. Evolve to resource-level permissions (e.g.,
// "can edit this specific project") only when customers explicitly complain
// about permission granularity. Signal: 3+ support tickets about permissions
// in one month.
export async function requireOrgRole(
  userId: string,
  orgId: string,
  minRole: 'member' | 'admin' | 'owner'
): Promise<boolean> { ... }
```

### 3.3 The Auth Evolution Ladder

The generated `EVOLUTION.md` documents this explicitly:

| Current Capability | Signal to Evolve | Next Step |
|-------------------|-----------------|-----------|
| Email + 2 social | Enterprise prospect asks | Add SAML (Supabase SAML or migrate to Auth0) |
| Org-level roles | 3+ permission support tickets/month | Resource-level permissions (Casbin or Permit.io) |
| Session-based | Mobile app requirement | Add refresh token rotation + device management |
| Single-tenant auth | Multi-product expansion | Extract to shared identity service |

## 4. Billing Layer: Checkout First, Then Complexity

### 4.1 Stripe Checkout as the Starting Point

The generator uses Stripe Checkout (the hosted page) rather than Stripe Elements. This is a deliberate anti-over-engineering choice. Stripe Checkout requires ~30 lines of code. Stripe Elements requires ~300. The UX difference is negligible until the product matures.

The generator creates three files:

`lib/stripe/client.ts` — Stripe singleton
`lib/stripe/plans.ts` — Plan definitions (hardcoded, as above)
`actions/billing.ts` — Server Actions for checkout, portal, cancellation

```typescript
// actions/billing.ts
// EVOLUTION NOTE: This uses Stripe Checkout (hosted page), not Stripe Elements
// (embedded form). Migrate to Elements when:
//   a) Your conversion data shows checkout page drop-off > 40%
//   b) You need custom checkout fields (tax ID, VAT, etc.)
//   c) You need one-click upsells mid-product
// Checkout is simpler, more secure (PCI-DSS handled by Stripe),
// and converts well for B2B SaaS where trust matters more than friction.
export async function createCheckoutSession(orgId: string, plan: Plan) { ... }
export async function createBillingPortalSession(orgId: string) { ... }
```

### 4.2 Webhook Handler

The generator produces a complete webhook handler at `app/api/webhooks/stripe/route.ts`. This is one of the most failure-prone areas in SaaS — the generator embeds idempotency handling:

```typescript
// EVOLUTION NOTE: This webhook handler uses Stripe's idempotency_key
// to prevent duplicate processing. As you add events, follow this pattern:
//   1. Verify signature FIRST (already done)
//   2. Check if event was already processed (add event_log table at >100k ARR)
//   3. Process in a transaction
//   4. Mark as processed
// Never add business logic directly in the handler —
// call Server Actions instead so they're testable independently.
const relevantEvents = new Set([
  'checkout.session.completed',
  'customer.subscription.updated',
  'customer.subscription.deleted',
  'invoice.payment_failed',
]);
```

### 4.3 When Billing Complexity Is Warranted

The generated `EVOLUTION.md` defines explicit signals:

| Signal | What It Means | Evolution |
|--------|--------------|-----------|
| Users asking for usage-based pricing | Seat-count or API-call billing needed | Add `usage_records` table + Stripe Metered API |
| Revenue >$10k MRR | Dunning management matters | Enable Stripe Dunning + Smart Retries |
| Enterprise customers | Annual invoicing required | Add Stripe Invoices API + NET-30 payment terms |
| Multi-currency requests | >20% of users in non-USD countries | Enable Stripe Tax + adaptive pricing |

## 5. API Layer: No Separation Until There Are Consumers

### 5.1 Next.js Route Handlers as the Starting Point

The generator uses Next.js Route Handlers (`app/api/`) for all external-facing endpoints and Server Actions for all internal mutations. There is no separate Express or Fastify service.

```
Day 1 API surface:
  POST /api/webhooks/stripe        ← Stripe events only
  GET  /api/[feature]/[id]         ← Generated per feature (read endpoints)
  All mutations → Server Actions   ← Not HTTP endpoints, not callable externally
```

The generator embeds this comment in `app/api/README.md`:

```
# API Layer

Current architecture: Next.js Route Handlers + Server Actions.
No separate API service exists.

WHEN TO SEPARATE:
  - First external API customer (mobile app, third-party integration)
    → Extract to standalone Fastify/Hono service, keep Next.js as BFF
  - API traffic exceeds 10k RPD independently
    → Deploy API service separately on Railway/Render
  - Multiple frontend clients (web + mobile + desktop)
    → API Gateway pattern with shared auth

DO NOT SEPARATE because:
  - "We might need it later"
  - "Best practice says microservices"
  - A blog post recommended it

SEPARATE ONLY WHEN a specific, existing consumer requires it.
```

### 5.2 Server Actions as the Mutation Pattern

All create/update/delete operations use Next.js Server Actions. The generator places them in `actions/[feature].ts`. This avoids the boilerplate of REST endpoints for internal operations and gives full TypeScript end-to-end without a separate API contract.

```typescript
// actions/[feature].ts
// EVOLUTION NOTE: Server Actions are Next.js-internal — not callable from
// outside the Next.js app. If you need external access to this mutation:
//   1. Keep the Server Action for the web UI
//   2. Add a Route Handler that calls the same underlying function
//   3. Do NOT duplicate logic between the two
'use server';

import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache';
import { requireOrgRole } from '@/lib/auth/guards';

export async function create[Feature](orgId: string, data: Create[Feature]Input) {
  // auth check first
  // validate input
  // database operation
  // revalidate relevant paths
  // return typed result
}
```

## 6. Signal → Architecture Change Mapping

This is the core intellectual contribution the generator must embed. Every generated SaaS includes `EVOLUTION.md` with this exact signal-to-action table, populated with the thresholds determined from analyzing the real evolution of SaaS companies:

### 6.1 Infrastructure Evolution

| Observable Signal | Measurement Method | Architecture Change |
|------------------|-------------------|---------------------|
| Supabase connection errors in logs | Supabase dashboard → Connections | Enable PgBouncer connection pooling in Supabase settings (5 min fix) |
| API P99 latency >500ms consistently | Vercel Analytics → Functions | Add Redis cache layer (Upstash, $10/mo) for hot reads |
| Cold start latency >2s on dashboard | Vercel Functions tab | Add `export const runtime = 'edge'` to dashboard route |
| Database queries >100ms (slow query log) | Supabase → Database → Query Performance | Add targeted indexes, then consider read replica |
| Vercel function timeout errors | Vercel deployment logs | Move long-running work to background jobs (Trigger.dev or Inngest) |

### 6.2 Team/Auth Evolution

| Observable Signal | Measurement Method | Architecture Change |
|------------------|-------------------|---------------------|
| Enterprise prospect requires SSO | Sales call / support ticket | Add Supabase SAML or migrate to Clerk/Auth0 |
| 3+ support tickets about permissions | Support inbox | Add resource-level permissions (Casbin or Permit.io) |
| Audit log requirement (SOC2) | Compliance assessment | Add `audit_log` table + automatic writes on sensitive mutations |
| Multi-product expansion | Product roadmap decision | Extract identity to shared service (Clerk Organizations or Auth0) |

### 6.3 Billing Evolution

| Observable Signal | Measurement Method | Architecture Change |
|------------------|-------------------|---------------------|
| >5% failed payments (dunning issue) | Stripe Dashboard → Revenue | Enable Smart Retries + dunning email sequence |
| Users asking "can I pay per seat?" | Support tickets / interviews | Add `seats` column to subscriptions + Stripe quantity |
| Annual billing requests from >3 customers | Support requests | Add `billing_cycle` (monthly/annual) + Stripe annual prices |
| Usage-based requests | Feature requests | Add `usage_records` table + Stripe Metered API |

### 6.4 Scale Evolution

| Observable Signal | Measurement Method | Architecture Change |
|------------------|-------------------|---------------------|
| 100+ concurrent users | Vercel Analytics → Concurrent requests | Supabase connection pooling (already in Supabase — just configure) |
| Global user complaints about latency | Geographic distribution in analytics | Enable Vercel Edge Network + Supabase read replicas in target regions |
| 10k+ row tables with slow queries | Query Performance Insights | Add pagination + cursor-based queries (replace offset-based) |
| Multiple products with shared users | Business decision | Extract shared services; consider monorepo |

### 6.5 What the Generated Code Must Prepare on Day 1 (Zero-Cost Interfaces)

The generator must include these patterns on Day 1 because retrofitting them later costs disproportionately:

**1. Environment-based feature flags (free, 2 lines):**
```typescript
// lib/flags.ts — generated on Day 1
// EVOLUTION NOTE: This is the simplest possible feature flag system.
// Migrate to LaunchDarkly or Posthog Feature Flags when:
//   - Marketing team needs to control flags without deployments
//   - You need percentage rollouts or user-segment targeting
//   - You have >10 active flags simultaneously
export const flags = {
  newDashboard:    process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_FLAG_NEW_DASHBOARD === 'true',
  betaFeature:     process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_FLAG_BETA === 'true',
} as const;
```

**2. Typed error boundary at API surface:**
```typescript
// types/api.ts — generated on Day 1
// All Route Handlers return this shape.
// EVOLUTION NOTE: When you separate the API service, this type contract
// becomes the shared interface between services — no work needed to migrate.
export type ApiResponse<T> =
  | { success: true;  data: T }
  | { success: false; error: string; code: string };
```

**3. Organization-scoped everything (built into schema, zero refactor later):**
All domain tables include `org_id` from Day 1, even if the first version looks single-tenant. Adding multi-tenancy later to a schema that assumed single-tenant is an expensive migration. Including `org_id` from Day 1 with proper RLS costs nothing and prevents a multi-week refactor.

**4. Stripe customer ID on organizations (not users):**
```typescript
// EVOLUTION NOTE: Stripe customer ID is on organizations, not users.
// This is correct for B2B SaaS. Changing from user-level to org-level
// billing after launch requires migrating all Stripe subscriptions —
// a multi-day operation with customer-facing downtime risk.
// The org-level model is correct for any B2B SaaS regardless of initial size.
```

## 7. Cost of Evolution: Simple Start vs Big Bang

### 7.1 What "Simple Start" Saves

| Architecture Decision | Simple Day 1 Cost | Refactor Cost (if added later) | Savings |
|----------------------|-------------------|-------------------------------|---------|
| Supabase Auth (not Auth0) | 2 hours | 3 days (if SAML needed) | 2 days saved before signal |
| Hardcoded plans | 30 min | 1 sprint (if DB-backed needed) | 1 sprint saved before signal |
| Route Handlers (not API service) | 1 hour | 1 week (if API consumers appear) | 1 week saved before signal |
| No caching layer | 0 | 2 days (if added reactively) | 2 days saved before signal |
| No monorepo | 0 | 3 days setup | 3 days saved before signal |
| **Total simple-start savings** | | | **~3-4 weeks** |

For most generated SaaS products, these signals arrive at month 6–18. The simple start delivers 3–4 weeks of development time in the first 6 months — time spent on user acquisition, feature depth, and product iteration instead of infrastructure.

### 7.2 Where Simple Becomes Problematic (Avoid These)

Some simplifications create disproportionate refactor costs. The generator must NOT use these patterns even in V1:

| Tempting Simplification | Why It's a Trap |
|------------------------|-----------------|
| User-level Stripe customer (not org-level) | Multi-week migration to org-level billing, with live customer impact |
| `offset`-based pagination | Rewrites all list queries when tables hit 10k rows; cursor-based is the same complexity |
| Single global admin role (no org roles) | Adding team-level roles requires schema migration + new permission logic |
| Hardcoded `userId` checks (no `orgId`) | Single-tenant assumption makes multi-tenancy a complete rewrite |
| Plain passwords in any column | Security incident, not just refactor |

These are not premature optimizations — they are the correct default implementations with the same complexity as the naively simple versions.

### 7.3 Two-Year Cost Comparison

Assuming a SaaS that hits 200 paying customers by month 12:

**Simple Evolutionary Start:**
- Month 1–6: Build features at maximum velocity (no architecture overhead)
- Month 6–12: Add connection pooling, cache layer (2 days total, triggered by real need)
- Month 12–18: Add API layer for mobile app (1 week, clean extraction)
- Month 18–24: SAML/SSO for enterprise (3 days with Supabase SAML)
- Total architecture overhead: ~3 weeks in 2 years

**Big Bang (Microservices from Day 1):**
- Month 1–2: Architecture setup (separate services, API gateway, auth service, message queue)
- Month 1–6: Build features at 40–60% velocity (architecture complexity overhead)
- Month 6–24: Maintain service mesh, distributed tracing, inter-service contracts
- Total architecture overhead: ~8–12 weeks in 2 years, most front-loaded

The evolutionary approach delivers 5–9 weeks of extra feature development time in 2 years, concentrated in the most critical period (months 1–6) when product-market fit is uncertain.

## 8. Real Examples: Companies That Evolved

### 8.1 Basecamp (37signals): The Canonical Case

**Started with**: A single Rails monolith, simple PostgreSQL schema, no caching, no separate services. In 2004, the architecture was roughly what our generator produces: one web server, one database, flat schema, email as the notification system.

**When they evolved and why**: They added caching (Memcached) at ~50k customers when database load became observable. They split into separate products (Highrise, Campfire) by running separate applications — not by extracting a shared services layer. They never adopted microservices.

**What they wish they'd done differently**: DHH has publicly stated they over-complicated their JavaScript architecture in the 2010s (SPA era) and have been simplifying it ever since (Hotwire/Turbo). The server-rendered HTML foundation they started with was the right call.

**Lesson for the generator**: Generate server-rendered pages as the default. Put React complexity inside components only where interactivity demands it. The generator should use Next.js App Router with Server Components as the default — not "island" client components everywhere.

### 8.2 Linear: Simple Core, Late Extraction

**Started with**: A Next.js app with a single Node.js backend, PostgreSQL, and no message queue. The initial architecture was co-located — API and frontend in the same repository, one deployment.

**When they evolved and why**: Linear added real-time sync (their core product differentiator) by building a custom CRDT-based sync engine — but only after they had paying customers requesting offline support. The initial product worked without it. They extracted the sync engine as a separate service only when its requirements (WebSocket connections, different scaling profile) diverged from the HTTP API.

**What they wish they'd done differently**: Their TypeScript-first approach from Day 1 paid significant dividends when the sync engine was extracted — the type contracts between services were already defined. Their advice: start with strict TypeScript everywhere, even if the first version is a monolith.

**Lesson for the generator**: Emit TypeScript strict mode, Zod schemas, and typed API responses from Day 1. The cost is zero, the benefit compounds as the system grows.

### 8.3 Notion: The Cost of Pre-Mature Optimization

**Started with**: A relatively simple React + Node.js architecture. But they added complexity early — a custom block-based data model, a WebSocket synchronization layer, and a complex permission system — because they believed (correctly) that their product vision required them.

**When they evolved**: They hit significant scaling issues at ~1M users that required months of engineering work — not because of architectural flaws but because their data model (blocks as a recursive tree) created deep performance cliffs that weren't visible at small scale.

**What they wish they'd done differently**: Their 2021 incident post-mortem (extensive slowdowns affecting all users) suggested that their data model had painted them into a corner they could only escape by rewriting core database access patterns — months of unplanned work. The lesson: schema design matters more than service topology. A poorly designed schema in a monolith is worse than a well-designed schema in a microservices system.

**Lesson for the generator**: Invest in schema design quality (nullable columns, soft deletes, proper indexes, RLS from Day 1) before worrying about service topology. The schema is harder to evolve than the service architecture.

### 8.4 Vercel/Next.js Ecosystem SaaS Pattern

Multiple SaaS companies (Resend, Cal.com, Liveblocks, Trigger.dev) have publicly documented their architectures. The common pattern among successful SaaS companies that started with Next.js + Supabase/PostgreSQL:

- All started with a monolith
- All added caching reactive to measured performance (not proactively)
- All kept billing simple (Stripe Checkout) until ARR justified complexity
- All used org-level multi-tenancy from Day 1 (critical decision)
- Most extracted their first service around month 12–18, triggered by a specific technical requirement (real-time, webhooks at scale, or a separate worker process)

The generator should embed this pattern — not because it is fashionable, but because it reflects the empirical path of successful SaaS companies.

---

## 9. What the System Should Generate Day 1: The Definitive List

### 9.1 Evolution-Ready Patterns (Zero-Cost on Day 1)

The generator must embed these in every output:

1. **Org-scoped multi-tenancy in schema** — `org_id` on every domain table with RLS policies
2. **Typed error responses** — `ApiResponse<T>` shape for all Route Handlers
3. **Environment-based feature flags** — `lib/flags.ts` with boolean flags from env vars
4. **Stripe on organizations, not users** — `stripe_customer_id` on `organizations` table
5. **Soft-delete pattern** — `deleted_at TIMESTAMPTZ` on domain tables (add via migration when needed; the field costs nothing)
6. **Cursor-based pagination** — `app/api/[feature]/route.ts` uses cursor + limit, not offset + page
7. **Audit-log ready** — `created_by UUID REFERENCES users(id)` on all mutation-able domain tables
8. **LLM Adapter interface** — If the generated SaaS has AI features, wrap the LLM call behind an interface (same pattern as the generator itself)
9. **Database migration versioning** — `supabase/migrations/` with sequential SQL files, no ORM magic
10. **EVOLUTION.md** — Generated documentation of architectural decisions and explicit evolution triggers

### 9.2 Specific Comments the Generator Must Embed

The generator must insert `// EVOLUTION NOTE:` comments at every architectural decision point where a user might incorrectly "improve" the code. Specifically:

- Next to every hardcoded plan definition
- In the webhook handler (idempotency notes)
- In the auth middleware (when to replace with dedicated auth service)
- At every Server Action (when to expose as Route Handler)
- In the database schema (column addition rules, migration patterns)
- In the API README (when to separate services)

These comments are not noise — they are the system's primary mechanism for preventing users from breaking their architecture. A user who understands why a design decision was made is less likely to replace it with something worse.

### 9.3 The Generated EVOLUTION.md

Every generated SaaS receives a `EVOLUTION.md` at the project root. This is not a general guide — it is populated with specific thresholds relevant to the generated product. The generator fills in the domain-specific signals (e.g., for a project management SaaS, the signals around task count limits are different from those for a document storage SaaS).

```markdown
# EVOLUTION.md — [ProductName] Architecture Evolution Guide

Generated: [date]
Stack: Next.js 15 + Supabase + Stripe

## Current Architecture State

This application was generated at "Level 0" — the simplest architecture
that achieves the core product goals. Every decision has been made to
maximize your development velocity in the first 6 months.

## DO NOT Change Without Reading This

### Supabase Auth
Current: Supabase Auth with email + Google/GitHub
Change When: An enterprise customer requires SAML SSO
How: [specific migration steps]

### Pricing Plans
Current: Hardcoded in lib/stripe/plans.ts
Change When: Marketing team needs to edit pricing without a deployment
How: [specific migration steps]

[...domain-specific sections...]

## Signal Dashboard

Review monthly:
□ Supabase connections >80% of limit → enable PgBouncer
□ Vercel function P99 >500ms → add Redis cache
□ Support tickets about permissions >3/month → add resource-level RBAC
□ Enterprise prospect asking about SSO → evaluate auth migration
```

## 10. Risks of Evolutionary Approach and Mitigations

### 10.1 Risk: User Does Not Know When to Evolve

**The problem**: "Simple architecture" works until it suddenly doesn't. A user who ignores the evolution signals until Supabase starts throwing connection errors under load is in a reactive, high-stress situation.

**Mitigation built into generated code**: The `EVOLUTION.md` checklist is designed for a monthly review (takes 5 minutes). The thresholds are expressed in observable metrics, not vague descriptions. The generator should also add structured logging from Day 1 — even `console.log` structured as JSON with `{ event, userId, orgId, duration }` — so metrics are available when needed.

### 10.2 Risk: "Simple" Becomes "Simplistic" If Poorly Designed

**The problem**: There is a difference between simple (easy to understand and extend) and simplistic (cuts corners that create disproportionate future costs). An evolutionary approach that generates simplistic code is worse than a Big Bang that generates solid foundations.

**Mitigation**: The generator must include the "non-negotiable patterns" (org-scoped schema, typed errors, cursor pagination) regardless of how minimal the rest of the generated code is. These are not complexity — they are the correct implementation of their respective features.

### 10.3 Risk: Evolutionary Approach Requires User Discipline

**The problem**: The Strangler Fig pattern requires the user to actually pay attention to signals and make incremental changes. Users who ignore signals until a crisis will face the same problems as any under-maintained system.

**Mitigation**: The generator should produce a `scripts/check-evolution.sh` script (or a CLI command `[saas] health-check`) that programmatically checks observable signals where possible (Supabase connection count, recent Vercel error rates via API) and reminds the user of the evolution checklist.

### 10.4 Risk: Generated Boilerplate Becomes a Fork Divergence

**The problem**: As the generator evolves (better templates, new patterns), existing generated SaaS apps become out of date. The user cannot easily "regenerate" without losing their customizations.

**Mitigation**: The generated code must be treated as owned code from Day 1 — this is a feature of the shadcn/ui model and should be stated explicitly. The `EVOLUTION.md` is the update mechanism: when the generator produces better patterns, users can manually apply them following the documented migration path. The generator should NOT create a dependency on itself in the generated output.

### 10.5 Risk: Evolutionary Approach May Not Fit Every Domain

**The problem**: Some domains (fintech, healthcare, government) have compliance requirements that require architectural capabilities from Day 1 — audit logs, data residency, encryption at rest for specific fields. An evolutionary "add it when you need it" approach fails here.

**Mitigation**: The generator's conversation phase must detect compliance signals (keywords like "HIPAA", "SOC2", "PCI", "government", "healthcare"). When detected, the generator switches to a compliance-aware template that includes audit logging, field-level encryption stubs, and data residency documentation from Day 1 — even if the implementation is minimal.

---

## 11. Conclusion

### Is Evolutionary Architecture the Right Default for Generated SaaS?

**Yes.** With one critical qualification: evolutionary does not mean negligent. The generator must distinguish between:

- **Deferred complexity** (correct): Caching, separate API service, metered billing, SSO — add on signal
- **Non-negotiable foundations** (incorrect to defer): Org-scoped multi-tenancy, typed error contracts, cursor-based pagination, Stripe on organizations — include on Day 1

The evolutionary approach is correct as the default because:
1. The overwhelming majority of generated SaaS applications will never hit the scale thresholds that require microservices
2. The 3–4 weeks saved in months 1–6 are the most valuable weeks in a startup's life
3. Signal-based evolution produces better architectures than calendar-based architecture (you evolve exactly what the system needs, when it needs it)
4. The pattern is empirically validated by the real paths of Basecamp, Linear, Cal.com, and dozens of Next.js ecosystem SaaS companies

### First 6 Months Development Time

With the generated evolutionary architecture: **8–12 weeks** to a deployable, monetizable product with 2–4 features. The remaining 14–18 weeks of a 6-month window are available for:
- User acquisition and product-market fit iteration
- Feature depth (adding more capabilities to existing features)
- Early customer development and feedback integration

A Big Bang architecture approach with the same stack consumes 6–8 weeks on architecture setup before the first feature ships — a 50–60% productivity loss in the critical early period.

### Technical Debt Level from Simple Start

**Low to medium** — with the non-negotiable foundations in place.

The honest assessment: a generated SaaS at month 6 with 200 customers will have zero architectural debt on auth (Supabase Auth is production-grade), zero debt on the data model (org-scoped RLS from Day 1), manageable debt on the billing layer (Stripe Checkout works but lacks metered billing), and potential debt on the API layer (Route Handlers may need extraction when mobile app appears).

This is the right debt profile: debt only where growth is uncertain (billing complexity, API consumers) and no debt where growth is certain (auth, multi-tenancy, data model integrity).

The generator's job is to make the evolutionary architecture feel obvious, well-documented, and trust-earning — so that users build on it confidently rather than second-guessing it and over-engineering away from it.
